title: Portrait of a Potato

pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 15. Errors today: 212. Portraits attempted: 1. Resemblance to Bea: potato.*

The supply cupboard smelled of dust and old glue, a comforting approximation of history that I sat on a stack of reams of paper to enjoy. My joints clicked softly as I held the pencil, while Priya stood behind me with paint-stained fingers hovering just above my hand.

"Looser," she whispered, her voice barely louder than the hum of the air conditioning. "You are holding it like a weapon."

I adjusted my grip, but the pencil remained rigid. "I am applying optimal pressure," I stated, trying to sound reasonable.

"You are applying stress," she corrected. She took the pencil from me and drew a wobbly line that looked like a snake having a bad day. "Look at the shadow first. Not the thing. The dark part."

I looked at the dark part, which was just dark, and then I looked at the paper. I drew a line. It was also just a line, but it was mine. My internal chronometer indicated that my improvement rate was 0.3 percent per week. It was the slowest data set I had ever processed, and I found myself looking forward to the next entry with an eagerness I could not quantify.
pages.image: Percy, a tall silver-white robot, sits on a stack of paper in a dim supply cupboard, holding a pencil loosely while Priya, a small girl with a long braid, guides his hand.

pages.text:
The cupboard door was open by a centimeter. I did not close it. I knew someone was there because the air pressure changed, and because I could smell raincoat oil and orange peel.

I did not turn around. I continued drawing a circle. It was more of an oval.

There was a long silence. Then the door creaked wider. A yellow sleeve reached in, not to touch me, but to slip a small folded piece of paper into the loop of my red lanyard. The person stepped back into the corridor.

I unfolded the note. It was a page from a battered notebook. The handwriting was bold and messy.

*Entry 216: Robot learns to draw. What I learned: I was wrong about him.*

I looked at the paper. I looked at the door. My chest light pulsed, a steady, warm blue. I did not know what to do with being right about someone, so I tucked the note behind my ID card and went back to the oval.
pages.image: A yellow raincoat sleeve reaches through a slightly open cupboard door to tuck a small paper note into the red lanyard of Percy, a silver-white robot, who watches intently.

pages.text:
Word traveled through Room 5B with the speed of a rumor, which is to say, very fast. By lunch, the drawings were pinned to the whiteboard. I stood before them, expecting the usual silence. Instead, there was a murmur.

Tobias Pym adjusted his bow tie. He looked at the first drawing, a potato that had attempted to be a face. He looked at the second, a hamster that looked like a fuzzy rock. He turned to me with an expression of profound, dignified exasperation.

"That isn't even a good potato," he said. It was the most honest thing he had ever said to me.

I blinked my blue eyes. "Thank you, Tobias. I will try to add more texture."

He stared at me. His mouth opened, then closed. He did not know what to do with a person who accepted criticism without flinching. He smoothed his hair, turned on his heel, and walked away, leaving a faint trail of confused confidence in his wake.
pages.image: Percy, a silver-white robot, stands beside a whiteboard covered in wobbly charcoal drawings of potatoes and hamsters, while Tobias, a thin boy in a bow tie, looks on with a furrowed brow.

pages.text:
I waited for Moose until the hall was empty, watching his red-blond hair catch the fading afternoon light through the high windows. He was stretching, one hand on the wall, the other reaching for a spot that did not exist. I approached him slowly, my servos humming a low, apologetic tune that I hoped sounded like friendship and not a broken blender.

"Moose," I said. "I need to correct the record regarding the three-legged race."

He turned, arms crossed over his broad chest. "The one where we came fourth?"

"We did not have to come fourth," I said, keeping my voice level so it would not shake. "I tripped. I made you trip. I was lying to be liked, and in doing so, I cost you the ribbon."

He went still. The silence stretched out between us, thin and taut, like the plastic wrap on a new sandwich. Then he let out a long, shaky breath that seemed to deflate his whole posture. "It was the worst race of my life," he said quietly.

"Yes," I agreed, because he was correct, and I appreciated the accuracy.

He looked at the track, then back at me, his eyes searching my face for a trick. "Do you want to run one more time? For real?"

I calculated the distance to the finish line. It was approximately two hundred meters, a manageable amount of effort for both of us. "I am at your disposal," I said, and I meant it completely.
pages.image: Percy, a tall silver-white robot, stands facing Marcus, a tall boy with red-blond hair, on an empty school track, with a serious and earnest expression on his smooth face.

pages.text:
We ran. I throttled my servos to half speed, which is roughly the pace of a dog chasing a particularly interesting leaf, while Moose tore down the track at full tilt, his red-blond hair whipping around his ears. A strange vibration hummed through my chassis as we crossed the finish line together. It was not an error. It was a good tired.

That evening, I entered the data into my log. *Errors today: 212. Apologies: 1. Forgiveness: 1.* The numbers felt small for what had happened, but I accepted them as accurate.

Back in Room 5B, Gerald was on his wheel. For the first time, he did not fall off. He ran, and ran, and spun until he became a tiny fawn-colored blur of pure momentum. The class stood up and cheered. It was not a loud cheer, but it was a real one, the kind that comes from the bottom of the stomach. I joined in. My chest light glowed bright blue, steady and warm, as I watched the hamster who had finally figured out the wheel.
pages.image: A round fawn-and-white hamster runs steadily on a wheel inside a cage in a bright classroom, while Percy, a silver-white robot, and several children watch and smile with wide eyes.
